newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-WEIRD SERIES BACK IN NEW YORK.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-WEIRD SERIES BACK IN NEW YORK.

text.p: "It's getting kind of eerie," says the New York Yankees' Wade Boggs.

Most Americans have barely begun thinking about the approaching Halloween holiday dedicated to all things ghostly and ghastly, but the Yankees, leading the Atlanta Braves three games to two in baseball's best-of-seven World Series, have been celebrating it for a while now.
Inexplicable stumbles, strange-but-true numbers and haunted houses where the home teams always lose have helped create one of the most unpredictable Series.
What new manifestations of the supernatural, the irrational and the just plain weird will arise as the World Series returns to New York this weekend for a game or two of Bronx cheers -- and boos?
Charlie Hayes hit the ball that turned into the only run of the Yankees' go-ahead game on Thursday, a ball which smooth-fielding Atlanta centre fielder Marquis Grissom made an error on.

"It was kind of a lucky play, like when the ball went through Alomar's legs," said Hayes, recalling Baltimore Orioles' Roberto Alomar's uncharacteristic error against the Yankees in the American League Championship Series.

And what invisible hand (shades of "the angel in the outfield," the 12-year-old fan who reached out and turned a Yankee out into a home run) directed closer Mark Wohlers' wild pitch on an intentional walk in Thursday's Game 5?
The Yankees have been talking about "destiny".
The Braves, who roared into their hometown up two games to none but left down 3-2, are feeling a bit cursed.
"We're not getting the breaks," manager Bobby Cox said. "This seems to be a game of inches and we're not getting the inch."
"Luck helps us, but most of it is a lot of heart," New York manager Joe Torre said.

One New York columnist even suggested that, just as trading away Babe Ruth is supposed to have left a curse on the Boston Red Sox, the Braves were cursed because of "the greed and tackiness" of the Atlanta Olympics.
The numbers seem to show that Atlanta should be leading.

The Yankees are batting .207, the Braves .256. The Yankees have 13 runs batted in, the Braves 24. The Yankees' earned run average is 4.30, the Braves' ERA is 2.15. Yankee pitchers have recorded 31 strikeouts, the Braves 40.
The difference has been in the heart and depth New York has produced in the clutch -- relief pitching and hitting off the bench.

Despite superior starting pitching, the Atlanta bullpen (Mark Wohlers, 6.75 ERA, Greg McMichael, 27.00 ERA, Steve Avery, 13.50 ERA) has not done the job. The Yankee bullpen has (John Wetteland, 0.00 ERA, Graeme Lloyd, 0.00 ERA, Jeff Nelson, 0.00 ERA, Mariano Rivera 2.45 ERA, David Weathers, 3.38 ERA).
Atlanta pinch-hitters have contributed nothing, going 0-for-20. The Yankees won Game 4 on Jim Leyritz's home run and Wade Boggs's bases-loaded walk. Both came off the bench.

But the home advantage New York would normally claim has been no advantage for the road-warrior Yankees, who lost their first two games here, then swept three in Atlanta to extend their record road streak to 8-0 this post-season.
"Hopefully, we'll turn into home warriors now," said rookie shortstop Derek Jeter.

It is just the second time, and first in 90 years, that the first five games of a World Series were won on the road. The previous time, that road wasn't very long since it was all played in Chicago, in 1906, between the Cubs and White Sox.
The New York fans can be very tough on visiting teams.
"It will be tougher on the Braves if we make it tougher," said Jimmy Key, New York's starter for Saturday's Game 6 and loser of Game 1. "The fans did their part, we just didn't do our part.
"Our crowd is very vocal, as you know, and gets into it. It's a fun atmosphere to play in. It can be intimidating for an opposing player. But it's up to us to put pressure on them."
"I'm sure the crowd will be on a high but we have to keep our emotions under control," said New York's hitting leader, Cecil Fielder (.421).
"It's the World Series, man," said Grissom, "I'm not worried about Yankee Stadium. We've got to go out there and play ball and see how good we can be."

Atlanta starter Greg Maddux noted that the Braves had their backs to the wall before, when they came back from a 3-1 deficit by winning three in a row against St Louis Cardinals in the National League Championship Series.
"I was in the same position last week and we came through," he said.

The four-time Cy Young Award winner would be followed to the mound in Sunday's Game 7, if the Braves can push it that far, by another former Cy Young winner, Tom Glavine, who clinched the Braves' championship last year.
"I do not think this is a commanding lead," said Torre. "The world champions are capable of winning two games in a row, and we face Maddux and Glavine."
